description: The Trinity, creation, the Incarnation, the last days of Jesus and salvation in Christianity.
content_html:
The Trinity: One God in Three Persons

Christianity teaches that there is one God who exists eternally as three distinct Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit. This is the doctrine of the Trinity. The three Persons are not three separate gods (polytheism) nor three modes of one God (modalism) — they are one God in a communion of being and love.

The Nicene Creed (325/381 CE) is Christianity’s most widely accepted doctrinal statement. It confesses the Father as creator of all things, the Son as “God from God, Light from Light, true God from true God,” and the Holy Spirit as “the Lord, the giver of life.” The Creed is used across Catholic, Orthodox and most mainline Protestant traditions, making it the closest thing to a universal Christian statement of belief.

Matthew 3:13–17 (the baptism of Jesus) shows all three Persons simultaneously: Jesus is baptised in the Jordan, the Holy Spirit descends as a dove, and the Father speaks from heaven — “This is my beloved Son.”

Key Fact

The Nicene Creed was agreed at Nicaea (325 CE) and Constantinople (381 CE). It is shared by Catholic, Orthodox and most Protestant churches. Matthew 3:13–17 is the key scriptural showing of all three Persons at once.

Creation: God and the Universe

Genesis 1–3 is the foundational Christian text on creation. Genesis 1 presents creation as six days of ordered making, culminating in humanity as the pinnacle. Genesis 2 gives a second, more intimate account focused on the first humans and their relationship with God. Genesis 3 introduces the Fall.

Christians interpret Genesis in divergent ways. A literal reading takes the six days as historical days. A metaphorical reading treats Genesis as theological poetry that conveys truths about God’s nature (creative, purposeful, benevolent) rather than a scientific sequence. John 1:1–18 adds the dimension that creation happened ‘through the Word’ — the eternal Son was the agent through whom all things were made, “and without him not one thing came into being.”

The Incarnation: God Becomes Human

The Incarnation is the belief that the second Person of the Trinity, the eternal Son (the Word or Logos), became human in the person of Jesus. John 1:14 states: “And the Word became flesh and lived among us.” 1 Timothy 3:16 calls this “the mystery of our religion” — God was manifested in flesh.

The Incarnation has enormous implications. It means Jesus is not merely a great teacher or prophet: he is the eternal God of the universe who chose to live a human life, to suffer and die. For Christians, this act of divine self-giving is the greatest expression of God’s love.

The Council of Chalcedon (451 CE) defined Jesus as “truly God and truly man,” with two natures in one Person. Catholic, Orthodox and most mainline Protestant churches affirm this. Some liberal Protestant theologians read the Incarnation as metaphorical — describing God’s deepest engagement with humanity rather than a literal metaphysical event. The Nicene Creed is the common anchor: “For us and for our salvation he came down from heaven... and was made man.”

The Last Days of Jesus

Luke 22–24 contains the account of Jesus’ last days. The sequence is: the Last Supper (Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples, saying “This is my body... this is my blood of the new covenant”); betrayal and arrest in Gethsemane; trial before the High Priest and Pilate; crucifixion on Golgotha; burial and then resurrection (the empty tomb and appearances to Mary, to the disciples on the Emmaus road, and to the eleven).

The Last Supper is the foundation of the Eucharist practised in churches today. The crucifixion and resurrection are together the central event of Christian history — the moment of salvation.

Salvation and Atonement

Salvation is the rescue of humanity from sin. Christians teach that sin — human rebellion against God’s will — separates humanity from God. Jesus’ death on the cross is understood as the means by which that separation is overcome.

Atonement theories explain how the cross achieves salvation. John 3:16 states: “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son, so that everyone who believes in him may not perish but may have eternal life.” Acts 4:8–12 records Peter asserting that “there is salvation in no one else” but Jesus Christ — a foundational claim about the uniqueness of Christ’s saving work.

Key Fact

John 3:16 — “God so loved the world that he gave his only Son” — is the key salvation verse. Acts 4:8–12 — Peter declares salvation is found in Christ alone. Both are essential 5-mark source references on salvation.

Christians agree that the cross achieves salvation but differ on how. Substitutionary atonement (popular in Reformed/evangelical Christianity): Jesus took humanity’s punishment in their place. Moral influence theory (associated with liberal Protestantism): the cross demonstrates God’s love so powerfully that it draws humanity to repentance. Christus Victor (common in Orthodox thinking): Jesus defeated the powers of sin, death and evil by dying and rising. All three agree that salvation comes through Christ; they differ on the mechanism.
exam_tip_html: This lesson covers a lot of ground — the Trinity, creation, Incarnation and salvation. In a 12-mark Discuss question, focus on one big idea at a time rather than listing all of them. For example: “The most important Christian belief is the Trinity” or “Salvation is only possible through Jesus Christ.” Develop both sides: those who agree (the Trinity organises all Christian theology; Acts 4:8–12 asserts Christ alone saves) and those who challenge (some liberal Christians are more pluralist; the Incarnation or resurrection may be considered more practically important). For the 5-mark Explain question, cite a specific verse: John 3:16 for salvation, John 1:14 for the Incarnation, or Matthew 3:13–17 for the Trinity. Vague references like ‘the Gospels’ do not earn the 5th mark.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The Trinity (Father, Son, Holy Spirit) is defined by the Nicene Creed (325/381 CE) and shown in Matthew 3:13–17; the Incarnation (John 1:14; 1 Timothy 3:16) teaches that the eternal Son became fully human.
  • Christians interpret Genesis 1–3 literally or metaphorically; John 1:1–18 adds that creation occurred through the eternal Word.
  • Salvation comes through Christ alone (Acts 4:8–12; John 3:16); atonement theories differ across denominations but all ground salvation in the cross and resurrection.

practice_questions.text: Outline three things Christians believe about the Trinity.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete points, e.g. (1) God is one being in three co-equal Persons; (2) The three Persons are Father, Son and Holy Spirit; (3) The Trinity is expressed in the Nicene Creed agreed at Nicaea (325 CE). Each must be a separately identifiable point.

practice_questions.text: Describe Christian beliefs about the Incarnation.
practice_questions.marks: May include: the eternal Son of God became human in Jesus; John 1:14 — 'the Word became flesh'; 1 Timothy 3:16 calls it 'the mystery of our religion'; Jesus is both fully God and fully human; the Incarnation is the basis for the Christmas celebration. Three accurate, relevant points.

practice_questions.text: Explain two ways Christians interpret the account of creation in Genesis.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed explanations. E.g. (1) Literal interpretation — some Christians, especially evangelical or fundamentalist Protestants, understand the six days as historical days; God created the universe in six 24-hour periods; this is sometimes called Young Earth Creationism; (2) Metaphorical interpretation — many mainline Protestants, Catholics and Orthodox Christians read Genesis as theological poetry that conveys truths about God's nature and humanity's relationship with God, rather than a scientific account; this allows compatibility with evolutionary biology. Development beyond naming the view required.

practice_questions.text: Explain two Christian beliefs about salvation, including a reference to a source of wisdom and authority.
practice_questions.marks: Two developed points, at least one named source. E.g. (1) Salvation comes through Christ alone — Acts 4:8–12 records Peter stating 'there is salvation in no one else' but Jesus; (2) God's motive for salvation is love — John 3:16 teaches that God gave his only Son so that all who believe would not perish but have eternal life. The 5th mark requires a named source: Acts 4:8–12, or John 3:16.

practice_questions.text: Outline three events in Jesus' last days as recorded in Luke 22–24.
practice_questions.marks: Three discrete events: (1) The Last Supper — Jesus shares bread and wine with his disciples; (2) Arrest and crucifixion — betrayed by Judas, tried by Pilate, crucified at Golgotha; (3) The resurrection — the empty tomb is found by the women; the risen Jesus appears to disciples.

practice_questions.text: 'The most important Christian belief is the resurrection of Jesus.' Discuss this statement.
practice_questions.marks: Mastering (10–12): Both sides fully developed with named sources; explicitly weighs; justified conclusion. FOR: without the resurrection, the cross is merely a tragic death; 1 Corinthians 15 argues 'if Christ has not been raised, your faith is futile'; resurrection is the basis of Christian hope. AGAINST: the Incarnation may be considered more foundational (without it the cross has no saving significance); others argue the Trinity is the organising belief; some emphasise the teaching of Jesus (e.g. the Sermon on the Mount) as equally central to Christian identity. Named sources: Luke 24; 1 Corinthians 15; John 3:16; Acts 4:8–12. Secure (7–9). Developing (4–6). Emerging (1–3).

What does 1 Timothy 3:16 describe as 'the mystery of our religion'?
options: God manifested in flesh — the Incarnation

flashcard_questions.q: What is the Nicene Creed and when was it agreed?
flashcard_questions.a: A statement of Christian Trinitarian faith, agreed at Nicaea (325 CE) and Constantinople (381 CE).

flashcard_questions.q: Which passage shows all three Persons of the Trinity simultaneously?
What does John 1:14 say about the Word?
flashcard_questions.a: That the Word became flesh and lived among us — the Incarnation.

flashcard_questions.q: What does 1 Timothy 3:16 call the Incarnation?
flashcard_questions.a: 'The mystery of our religion' — God manifested in flesh.

flashcard_questions.q: How did Jesus describe his Last Supper actions?
flashcard_questions.a: He said the bread was his body and the wine was his blood of the new covenant.

flashcard_questions.q: What does Acts 4:8–12 teach about salvation?
flashcard_questions.a: That salvation is found in Jesus Christ alone — there is no other name under heaven.

flashcard_questions.q: What does John 3:16 say about God's motive for salvation?
flashcard_questions.a: God so loved the world that he gave his Son — all who believe have eternal life.
The reconciliation of humanity with God through Christ's death, removing the barrier of sin.

flashcard_questions.q: What are the three main theories of the atonement?
flashcard_questions.a: Substitutionary, moral influence, and Christus Victor.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between a literal and metaphorical reading of Genesis?
flashcard_questions.a: Literal: six historical days. Metaphorical: theological truth about God, not a scientific account.

flashcard_questions.q: What does John 1:1–18 add to the creation account?
flashcard_questions.a: That creation happened through the eternal Word (Son), and nothing was made without him.

glossary_terms.definition: The Christian belief that one God exists as three distinct, co-equal and co-eternal Persons: Father, Son and Holy Spirit.
The authoritative statement of Christian faith composed at the First Council of Nicaea (325 CE) and completed at the First Council of Constantinople (381 CE), expressing belief in the Trinity.
The Christian doctrine that the eternal Son of God took on human flesh in the person of Jesus Christ, becoming fully God and fully human.
Jesus' last meal with his disciples before his arrest, at which he shared bread and wine and instructed them to 'do this in remembrance of me' (Luke 22:19), founding the Christian Eucharist.
In Christian theology, the reconciliation of humanity with God through Jesus Christ's death and resurrection, rescuing humanity from sin and its consequences.
The theological concept that Jesus' death on the cross reconciles or 'at-ones' humanity with God, paying the price for sin.
